acceptance_criteria.criterion: statusPollTimer is pushed into _orchLogPreviewCleanups via a cleanup callback that calls clearInterval(statusPollTimer).
The cleanup line is positioned after the setInterval(...) call and inside the if (runStatusFilename) block.
When renderOrchestrator() is re-invoked, the _orchLogPreviewCleanups drain loop clears the interval (verifiable by code inspection or unit test).
No behavioural regression — the orchestrator view loads, polls status, and clears correctly.

summary: Added one line after the setInterval(...) call inside the if (runStatusFilename) block in orchestrator.js: `_orchLogPreviewCleanups.push(function () { clearInterval(statusPollTimer); });`. This registers the statusPollTimer interval for cleanup when renderOrchestrator() re-renders, preventing orphaned intervals. All 2204 tests pass with no regressions.

comments.note: The statusPollTimer interval already self-cancels inside the callback (via clearInterval(statusPollTimer) when status resolves or MAX_STATUS_POLLS is reached). The new _orchLogPreviewCleanups entry provides a safety net for the case where the user navigates away or re-renders before the timer self-terminates. This dual-cancel pattern is correct and intentional.

orchestrator.js lines 180–181: refreshQueue() also drains _orchLogPreviewCleanups directly (not just renderOrchestrator()). This means the statusPollTimer cleanup registered after startBtn click will also be cleared by the next queue refresh — which may clear it prematurely if a queue poll fires before the status poll resolves. This is pre-existing behaviour and out of scope for this WP, but worth noting for future review.
